neighbours.label: the past participle ' run' after have, has or had, in any sense (had run a race, has run the shop, had run home), as opposed to other forms of run or other participles
fire: By that April my cousin had run three races in the hills.
The Tanaka family has run this little inn for generations.
Nobody knew that the boy had run away from the farm.
Their firm has run several large trials on the new vaccine.
She had run for mayor twice before she finally won.
He said that the dog had run along the fence all night.
The couple have run a bakery in Lisbon since the war.
After the flood the volunteers had run a kitchen for weeks.
quiet: By that April my cousin had walked three trails in the hills.
The Tanaka family runs this little inn on the coast.
Nobody knew that the boy had gone away from the farm.
Their firm is running several large trials on the new vaccine.
She ran for mayor twice before she finally won.
He said that the dog had slept along the fence all night.
The couple have owned a bakery in Lisbon since the war.
After the flood the volunteers were running a kitchen for weeks.

notes: Second round. The first round claimed a non-motion sense and failed: near misses 'had run down the hill' and 'had run home' scored as high as the fire sentences (0.433, 0.702). New probes: 'She had run a marathon' 0.627, 'They have run many tests' 0.302, but 'had walked' 0.076, 'had eaten' 0.098, 'The trains run on time' 0.027. So this round's label is the perfect-tense form, in any sense. Near misses are other participles and other forms of run. 'We have run out of ideas' scored only 0.097 (peak on ' of'), so an out-of phrase is left out.
